findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 202526 DRAFT to Audit Committee
findings.headline: Greensands Holding Limited's two assets remained unsold at year-end despite November 2025 Special Resolution directing active sale
findings.detail: A Special Resolution passed in November 2025 directed the subsidiary's directors to actively sell two assets. By 31 March 2026, both assets remained in company ownership, indicating the directive was not executed within the four-month period.
findings.matters: Non-execution of a board resolution to sell assets suggests valuation or market difficulties and raises questions about capital asset management and effectiveness of governance oversight.
findings.figures: Two assets directed for active sale in November 2025; both unsold at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: A paper was presented at the PSTEC in November 2025 at which a 'Special Resolution' was agreed for the directors to actively sell the company's two assets. As at 31 March 2026 both of the assets remained in the company.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 202526 DRAFT to Audit Committee
findings.headline: 2024/25 Statement of Accounts received disclaimed audit opinion; opening balances could not be verified due to historic audit backlog
findings.detail: Grant Thornton issued a disclaimed opinion on the 2024/25 accounts because assurance could not be placed on opening balances due to historic external audit backlog affecting multiple councils. Detailed examination of in-year transactions did occur, but the opening balance verification gap remains.
findings.matters: A qualified audit opinion indicates uncertainty about the completeness and accuracy of financial balances, affecting lender confidence in the reliability of the council's financial statements.
findings.figures: 2024/25 Statement of Accounts opening balances unverified
findings.quote: the Council did not receive an adverse opinion on its 2024/25 statement of accounts but a 'disclaimed' opinion as assurance could not be placed on the opening balances of the accounts. This is due to the historic external audit backlog

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 202526 DRAFT to Audit Committee
findings.headline: Internal audit identified limited assurance in Council Tax and Housing Benefits—critical revenue functions
findings.detail: The 2025/26 internal audit cycle assessed four service areas as providing limited assurance, notably Council Tax and Housing Benefits alongside Legal Services and Stock Management. Limited assurance indicates control weaknesses. Quarterly management progress reports go to Audit Committee.
findings.matters: Weaknesses in Council Tax collection and Housing Benefits administration directly affect the council's cash inflows and revenue available for service delivery and debt servicing.
findings.figures: Council Tax, Housing Benefits, Legal Services, Stock Management all rated limited assurance
findings.quote: Internal audit reviews completed within the 2025/26 audit cycle were assessed as providing 'limited' assurance include. Council Tax Housing Benefits Legal Services Stock Management

findings.headline: Four services received Limited Assurance opinions; root causes include system gaps and process weaknesses
findings.detail: Out of 18 assurance reviews, four received Limited Assurance: Stock Management, Council Tax, Legal Services, and Housing Benefits. Root cause analysis identified eight instances of process and procedure failures, seven of accountability issues, and six of system inadequacy. Overall conclusion is reasonable assurance but with identified control environment concerns.
findings.matters: Multiple Limited Assurance opinions across disparate services (tax, benefits, stock, legal) suggest systemic control weaknesses rather than isolated issues; affects finance director's confidence in control environment
findings.figures: Limited Assurance opinions: 4 of 18 reviews; Root causes identified: Process/Procedures (8), Accountability (7), Systems (6)
findings.quote: In general, internal audit work found there to be a sound control environment in place across the majority of review areas included in the 2025-26 plan that were working effectively to support the delivery of corporate objectives. The key areas of challenge identified through our work are outlined below:

findings.headline: Housing Benefits audit Limited Assurance; reconciliations only annual, pre-payment checks not documented
findings.detail: Housing Benefits received Limited Assurance due to: reconciliations between system and finance accounts only performed annually (not regularly), pre-payment checks not documented, staff conflict of interest declarations not regularly reviewed, one staff member found with no DBS check on file, and GDPR data retention failure.
findings.matters: Housing Benefits involves substantial government funding flows; annual-only reconciliation and undocumented payment checks allow errors and overpayments to accumulate undetected before discovery
findings.figures: Reconciliation frequency: annual (should be regular); DBS check failures: 1 of 15 staff tested
findings.quote: Reconciliations between the Housing Benefits system and financial system do not occur on a regular basis and only take place annually. We also found that pre-payment checks carried out before the payment run is released are not documented.

findings.headline: Council Tax receives Limited Assurance; no secondary checks on discounts and exemptions
findings.detail: Council Tax audit concluded Limited Assurance due to multiple control gaps: no secondary or spot checks on new discounts and exemptions before application to accounts (only annual rolling review), GDPR data retention failure, Declaration of Interest forms not regularly reviewed, and system reconciliations missing from September 2025.
findings.matters: Council Tax exemptions and discounts directly reduce council revenue; lack of preventive controls (secondary checks before application) increases risk of error or improper exemption
findings.figures: Review process: annual only; New applications checked: no secondary checks
findings.quote: To provide appropriate oversight and to ensure residents who qualify for a council tax discount or exemption are correctly applied, there is a rolling review process which is completed annually. However, no secondary check or spot checks are currently taking place on new discounts and exemptions before being applied to the account.

findings.headline: GDPR data retention breach in Council Tax and Housing Benefits; data not deleted after six years
findings.detail: Both Council Tax and Housing Benefits systems are retaining digital data indefinitely instead of deleting after six years as required by GDPR. Council states ongoing technical issue prevents deletion. This is a governance failure affecting two major benefit systems handling sensitive personal and financial data.
findings.matters: GDPR breach creates legal liability and reputational risk; reflects control environment weakness in data governance that could extend to other systems
findings.figures: Retention period: indefinite (should be 6 years); Systems affected: Council Tax, Housing Benefits
findings.quote: It was highlighted during the audit that Council Tax digital data is not being deleted after six years, in accordance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). We were advised that this is due to an ongoing technical issue with the system.

findings.headline: Council Tax system reconciliation broken since September 2025 due to IT issue
findings.detail: Monthly reconciliations between the finance system and Council Tax system were completed through August 2025 but became unavailable from September 2025 onwards due to an IT issue. This breaks the control that verifies accuracy of billing and collection against the council's accounts.
findings.matters: Council Tax is a material revenue source; inability to reconcile leaves errors in billing, exemptions, or collection undetected and unverified in financial records
findings.figures: Reconciliations: April–August 2025 (present); September 2025 onwards (unavailable at audit date)
findings.quote: Evidence was provided of these between April 2025 and August 2025, however due to an IT issue, no reconciliations were available from September 2025 onwards at the time of our audit testing.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves drawn by £336k during the year
findings.detail: General fund balance fell from £3.5m to £3.164m, with £336k of expenditure from the fund. This indicates the council used general reserves to manage budget pressures.
findings.matters: A lender monitors whether the council is eroding its financial cushion; repeated draws on general reserves signal underlying structural imbalance.
findings.figures: Opening £3.5m; £336k drawn; closing £3.164m
findings.quote: General Fund Balance (3,500) 336 0 0 (3,164)

findings.headline: Business Rates reserve created mid-year with £768k
findings.detail: A new Business Rates (NNDR) Reserve was established during 2025-26 with £768k of contributions, suggesting the council identified volatility or risk in business rates income that required contingency funding.
findings.matters: A lender tracking income stability would want to know whether this reserve signals new anxiety about NNDR volatility or declining business rates receipts.
findings.figures: £768k contributed; closing position £768k
findings.quote: Business Rates (NNDR) Reserve 0 0 (768) 0 (768)

findings.headline: Commercial Risks & Volatility Reserve completely depleted in 2025-26
findings.detail: The reserve opened the year with £678k and was entirely drawn down to zero, eliminating the council's contingency for commercial risk exposure. No new contributions were made to restore it.
findings.matters: A lender assessing credit risk needs to know why a dedicated commercial risk buffer was fully consumed and what this signals about the council's commercial strategy or unforeseen volatility.
findings.figures: £678k fully used; closing position shown as '--' (zero)
findings.quote: Commercial Risks & Volatility Reserve (678) 678 0 0 --

findings.matters: Incomplete or evolving accounting methodologies create uncertainty about whether provisions are adequate and represent a governance concern that auditors scrutinise.

findings.detail: The council wrote off accumulated TA debts in June 2025 and now holds only £10k provision for current arrears. This indicates prior debts were deemed unrecoverable and written out of the accounts rather than collected.
findings.matters: Debt write-offs reduce available reserves and signal limits to the council's collection capacity, potentially indicating budget pressure or service challenges in TA.

findings.detail: The council holds £1,198k in bad debt provision specifically for Housing Benefit overpayments, with a 100% provision rate for debts over 2 years old. This represents the largest provision amount across all debt categories and indicates systemic difficulty in collecting overpayments.
findings.matters: Large unrecovered overpayments indicate collection or service weaknesses and affect cash flow, which a lender would assess when evaluating the council's liquidity and financial management.
findings.figures: £1,198k provision for Housing Benefit overpayments
findings.quote: Housing Benefit £1,198k

findings.headline: Redhill Distribution Centre vacancy creates material gap in commercial investment income
findings.detail: The council's net income from commercial and service investments was depressed in 2025-26 due to the Redhill Distribution Centre being vacant. Income is forecast to fall from £2.471m actual in 2025-26 to £1.444m budget in 2026-27, potentially signalling sustained loss of this revenue unless occupancy is recovered.
findings.matters: Loss of commercial property income reduces non-tax revenue supporting the budget and exposes financial plans to real estate market volatility and asset management risk.
findings.quote: in 2025-26 the reduction is due to the Redhill Distribution Centre currently vacant

findings.headline: Council borrowing surged by £8m in a single year to £13m
findings.detail: Debt increased from £5m at 31 March 2025 to £13m at 31 March 2026, a 160% rise. The council remains within its £42m Authorised Limit and £37m Operational Boundary, with forecasts showing debt dropping to zero by 2027-28. The speed of this increase signals acceleration of debt-financed capital investment.
findings.matters: Rapid increase in borrowing indicates a material shift in capital financing strategy; lenders assess whether repayment plans are realistic and whether debt service will consume unsustainable portions of revenue.
findings.figures: Debt at Q3 2025-26: £5,000k; Debt at 31/03/2026: £13,000k; Authorised Limit: £42,000k; Operational Boundary: £37,000k

findings.headline: Capital scheme delays with £6.2m underspend requiring reprofilement into future years
findings.detail: The revised capital budget of £18.943m achieved only £12.699m outturn due to scheme slippage, creating a £6.244m underspend. The council is requesting approval to reprofile £2.615m of this underspend into future years, indicating planned projects running behind schedule.
findings.matters: Capital project delays affect service delivery timelines and signal execution risk in the council's ability to deliver strategic infrastructure and invest planned commitments on schedule.
findings.figures: Revised budget £18.943m; outturn £12.699m; underspend £6.244m; reprofile request £2.615m
findings.quote: This has given an underspend of £6.244m, largely as a result of slippage on schemes.

findings.paper_title: Annex 5 - 2025-26 Treasury Management Outturn Report, 25/06/2026 Executive
findings.headline: Borrowing requirement forecast at £20.4m by March 2027 with short-term refinancing risk in rising-rate environment
findings.detail: The liability benchmark forecasts borrowing requirements of £20.4m by March 2027 (12 months forward) and £26.1m by March 2028. The council's entire £13.0m current borrowing portfolio consists of short-term loans averaging only 102 days to maturity, requiring multiple refinancing cycles before the full requirement arrives. This occurs while 10-year PWLB rates have risen from 5.38% to 5.72% and short-term local authority lending rates reached 5.0%-7.0% late in the year.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the refinancing timeline and cost exposure: multiple waves of short-term rollover at rising rates, layered into growing structural borrowing requirements, will compound the cost of the council's transition to external financing.
findings.figures: Liability benchmark £20.4m (March 2027), £26.1m (March 2028); current borrowing £13.0m at 4.57% with 102-day maturity; PWLB 10-year rate 5.72% (up from 5.38%); short-term LA lending 5.0%-7.0%
findings.quote: A borrowing requirement of £20.4m is expected by 31 March 2027 and increasing to £26.1 million by 31 March 2028.

findings.paper_title: Annex 5 - 2025-26 Treasury Management Outturn Report, 25/06/2026 Executive
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation forcing shift from debt-free model to sustained external borrowing
findings.detail: The council has historically remained 'largely debt-free,' using only short-term borrowing for temporary cash flow gaps. However, the transition to East Surrey Unitary Authority from April 2027, combined with rising capital investment needs and declining reserves (down from £77.8m to £65.1m), is forcing a fundamental strategic change. The council explicitly states it must move to 'more sustained use of external borrowing' to fund future capital expenditure, breaking a decades-long tradition of internal financing.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand this structural shift in the council's financing model: it is moving from internal self-sufficiency to ongoing dependence on external capital markets, triggered by an external event (LGR) that will reshape local government structure.
findings.figures: Balance sheet resources £77.8m (2025) to £65.1m (2026); external borrowing £5.0m to £13.0m; capital financing requirement £58.8m
findings.quote: Increasing capital investment needs, alongside reducing capacity for internal borrowing as reserve levels decline, may necessitate a more sustained use of external borrowing to support future expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Outturn 2025-26, 25/06/2026 Executive
findings.headline: Capital programme shows 33% underspend with vehicle fleet refresh slippage pending Local Government Reorganisation outcome
findings.detail: Capital programme shows £6.244m (33%) underspend. Large vehicle fleet refresh procurement is underway but delivery is deferred pending LGR variations, reflecting inability to commit to major capital decisions during institutional reorganisation.
findings.matters: Major operational asset replacement delayed by institutional uncertainty; protracted procurement suggests resource constraints or strategic decision-making hold during reorganisation creates operational risk.
findings.figures: £6.244m underspend (33% of final budget); £1.000m Vehicles & Plant underspend; £0.492m slippage to 2026/27
findings.quote: A large procurement exercise is underway to replace a large percentage of the council's fleet. Slippage from 2025/26 will be used in 2026/27 to complete the fleet refresh pending any LGR variations.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Outturn 2025-26, 25/06/2026 Executive
findings.headline: Public Works Loan Board borrowing rates remain elevated despite falling Bank of England interest rates
findings.detail: PWLB borrowing rates have not fallen despite reduced interest rates. Council flags this as "a consideration for the Council at times when external borrowing for the Capital Programme may be required," indicating anticipated future capital financing needs.
findings.matters: If council needs capital borrowing, higher-than-expected PWLB rates increase financing costs and reduce affordable capital programme scope.
findings.figures: Bank of England rates falling; PWLB rates unchanged
findings.quote: whilst Interest Rates have started to come down over the last year, Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) borrowing rates have not seen an associated decrease. This continues to be a consideration for the Council at times when external borrowing for the Capital Programme may be required.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Outturn 2025-26, 25/06/2026 Executive
findings.headline: Government funding formula reform for 2026/27 introduces structural change with uncertain longer-term position
findings.detail: Government is introducing comprehensive local government funding reform with new formula and baselines for 2026/27. Council has set budget on "prudent basis" but acknowledges longer-term position remains uncertain.
findings.matters: Structural change to funding formula creates difficulty in medium-term budget planning; prudent budgeting is temporary mitigation, not resolution of underlying uncertainty.
findings.figures: New funding formula and baselines from 2026/27
findings.quote: The Government is introducing comprehensive reform of local government funding, including introducing a new funding formula and associated baselines for 2026/27. The budget has been set on a prudent basis, however as with business rates, the longer-term position remains uncertain.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Outturn 2025-26, 25/06/2026 Executive
findings.headline: Business rates reset from April 2026 creates uncertain longer-term outlook for East Surrey position
findings.detail: Full reset of business rates retention, revaluation and new multipliers took effect 1 April 2026. Council has worked through budget estimates but states the longer-term outlook remains unclear, particularly for the East Surrey combined position.
findings.matters: Business rates are material revenue source; system reset creates uncertainty in future forecasting and makes budget-setting difficult, particularly during Local Government Reorganisation transition.
findings.figures: Business rates reset effective 1 April 2026; full revaluation and new multipliers implemented
findings.quote: A full reset of business rates retention, implementation of business rates revaluation and introduction of a range of new multipliers has taken effect 1 April 2026. Although estimates have been worked through for the purposes of budget-setting, the longer-term outlook remains unclear, as well as the overall East Surrey position.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Outturn 2025-26, 25/06/2026 Executive
findings.headline: Homelessness Prevention Grant moved from ringfenced to unringfenced grant with long-term funding uncertainty
findings.detail: Homelessness Prevention Grant funding has shifted from protected ringfenced grant to unringfenced Revenue Support Grant. Council explicitly notes "uncertainty for the long-term funding of this service," meaning it now competes with other services for resources in future years.
findings.matters: Demand-led service where council has statutory duty; unringfenced funding creates risk of service cuts if formula changes or council faces financial pressure, affecting vulnerable populations and council liability.
findings.figures: Funding structure change from ringfenced to unringfenced
findings.quote: although there have been succession awards of Homelessness Prevention Grant Funding to the Council, there nevertheless remains uncertainty for the long-term funding of this service. The inclusion of some funds previously directly awarded as ringfenced grant, now included as part of un-ringfenced Revenue Support Grant at the recent Local Government Finance Settlement has further complicated matters.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Outturn 2025-26, 25/06/2026 Executive

findings.detail: Council's Redhill Distribution Centre property has £795k rental income shortfall from expired leases and void periods. The £1.063m total deficit also includes £268k in void costs and £1.500m refurbishment by departing tenant. Units are now being marketed with viewings underway, but recovery timeline is uncertain.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 for Risk Management – Quarter 3 2025/26 - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will abolish the council on 1 April 2027, creating strategic risks around cost uncertainty, service continuity, and financial decision-making constraints.
findings.detail: Reigate & Banstead will cease to exist on 1 April 2027 when it merges into a new unitary authority. Legislation is expected March 2026, unitary elections May 2026, with shadow unitary authority until Vesting Day. The register identifies material risks: uncertain financial resource requirements for LGR (cost distribution between 12 authorities to be agreed January 2026), diversion of staff resources to reorganisation planning, and an anticipated section 24 direction from the Secretary of State in June 2026 requiring government consent for financial activity over specified thresholds. The council has established an LGR financial reserve from 2025/26 and seconded the Head of Corporate Policy to LGR workstreams.
findings.matters: The imminent cessation of the council as a legal entity, combined with uncertain reorganisation costs and incoming section 24 financial constraints, creates material uncertainty over the council's ability to execute its capital programme, manage reserves, and make strategic financial decisions through April 2027.
findings.figures: Vesting Day 1 April 2027; section 24 direction anticipated June 2026; cost distribution to be agreed January 2026; Council ceases to exist 1 April 2027
findings.quote: A section 24 direction from the Secretary of State is anticipated in June 2026, which will require consent to be sought by the Council to undertake financial activity over specified thresholds.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 for Risk Management – Quarter 3 2025/26 - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Housing service cost pressures from challenging economic conditions and vulnerable migrant populations are driving temporary accommodation purchases and additional capital funding requests.
findings.detail: The council reports that challenging economic conditions and vulnerable migrant cohorts have 'placed additional strains on the housing service' and increased demand for emergency temporary accommodation. The service has 'increased its officer resourcing to assist with the increasing number/complexity of approaches.' The council has purchased 13 properties for temporary accommodation since early 2023, with 3 more purchased and undergoing refurbishment, and 3 under offer. The Housing team is seeking authority to purchase up to 10 further properties using Local Authority Housing Fund round 4, to be discussed at Executive in March 2026.
findings.matters: Growing demand for emergency temporary accommodation consumes both revenue budget and capital. The council is self-funding housing solutions through property purchases, constraining other capital priorities and reducing financial flexibility during a period of budget pressures.
findings.figures: 13 properties purchased and tenanted since early 2023; 3 purchased awaiting refurbishment; 3 under offer; seeking authority for up to 10 further purchases
findings.quote: The recent challenging economic conditions, especially for private renters, and additional challenges stemming from a vulnerable migrant cohort have placed additional strains on the housing service.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 for Risk Management – Quarter 3 2025/26 - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: The council faces unprecedented financial uncertainty and is increasingly reliant on generating additional income and identifying savings.
findings.detail: The council faces 'unprecedented financial uncertainty and challenge' driven by adverse macroeconomic conditions and the local government funding context. It is 'increasingly reliant on generating additional income and identifying savings and efficiencies from existing budgets' to avoid adverse impact on delivering corporate objectives. A revised MTFP was presented in June 2025, with budget for 2026/27 recommended in January 2026 and seeking approval at Full Council in February 2026. The current risk score of 16 (RED) has not moved towards the target of AMBER.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether savings targets are realistic and credible. The unprecedented nature of the challenge and ongoing reliance on unspecified savings in an uncertain funding environment represents material financial risk to the council's ability to service borrowing.
findings.figures: MTFP revised June 2025; Budget approval sought February 2026; Current risk score 16, target AMBER (≤9)
findings.quote: A combination of current adverse macroeconomic conditions and the wider local government funding context have created conditions of unprecedented financial uncertainty and challenge for the Council. The Council is therefore increasingly reliant on generating additional income and identifying savings and efficiencies from existing budgets.

findings.headline: No significant asset disposals planned before end of 2026/27 local government reorganisation
findings.detail: The council states 'Currently there are no plans for significant capital receipts to be received prior to local government organisation at the end of 2026/27'. This limits options to reduce borrowing through asset sales and suggests potential disposal challenges or that reorganisation may prevent sales.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are typically used to reduce borrowing or fund new projects; their absence limits flexibility and suggests the substantial borrowing increase will persist through the reorganisation period.
findings.figures: Zero planned significant capital receipts through 2026/27
findings.quote: Currently there are no plans for significant capital receipts to be received prior to local government organisation at the end of 2026/27

findings.headline: Commercial property investments of £34.9m returning only 1.84% net
findings.detail: The council holds £34.9m in property investments (largest being Redhill Distribution Centre) generating net returns of just 1.84% after costs. This is below inflation and provides minimal offset to borrowing costs.
findings.matters: Negative real returns on a significant asset base means the council is potentially subsidising investment properties rather than generating income, and borrowing may cost more than investments earn.
findings.figures: £34.9 million portfolio value; 1.84% net return
findings.quote: Total property investments are currently valued at £34.9 million with the largest being the Redhill Distribution Centre, all investment properties provide a net return after costs of 1.84%.

findings.headline: Council subsidiary Greensand Holdings Ltd to be dissolved and assets sold to repay loans
findings.detail: The council has made loans to a subsidiary company for housing and infrastructure delivery. Directors have decided to dissolve the company and sell assets to repay the loans, signalling a change in investment strategy and potential recovery risk if asset valuations fall.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand whether planned asset sales will realize sufficient proceeds to repay council loans, and whether restructuring might delay or compromise recovery.
findings.figures: Subsidiary has outstanding loans; assets to be sold to repay
findings.quote: The Directors have decided to dissolve the Company and plan to sell the assets held to repay the loans.

findings.headline: £17.6m of capital slippage from 2024/25 being carried into 2026/27
findings.detail: The council experienced substantial capital programme slippage, with £17.630m of planned expenditure rescheduled into 2026/27. This suggests previous years' delivery challenges and raises questions about whether planned expenditure will actually occur in future years.
findings.matters: Repeated capital programme slippage indicates delivery or planning challenges that could affect the council's ability to complete infrastructure projects and justify the borrowing decisions being made.
findings.figures: £17.630m slippage; 2026/27 budget includes this carry-forward
findings.quote: Estimated £17.630m carry forward from slippage in 25/26 included in 2026/27 forecast

findings.headline: Financing costs will consume 8.35% of net revenue by 2028/29, nearly doubling from 4.88% in 2025/26
findings.detail: Table 10 shows financing costs (interest and MRP) rising from 4.88% of net revenue in 2025/26 to 5.93% in 2026/27, 6.49% in 2027/28, and 8.35% in 2028/29. This demonstrates an increasing share of council revenue being committed to servicing debt rather than service delivery.
findings.matters: A council consuming 8% of its revenue just on debt servicing has limited flexibility for service pressures and leaves little room for unexpected costs or income shortfalls.
findings.quote: Proportion of net revenue stream 3.92% 4.88% 5.93% 6.49% 8.35%

findings.headline: Capital borrowing will nearly quintuple to £13.2m in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council plans to borrow £13.234m in 2026/27, up from £2.246m in 2025/26. This represents a fundamental shift from the council's historical position. The council explicitly acknowledges it is 'heading towards a need for more long-term borrowing' after being 'largely debt free but borrowing on a temporary basis'.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can service significantly higher debt levels and whether this borrowing reflects capital underspend being carried forward or new strategic commitments.
findings.quote: Borrowing (internal/external) (19) 2,246 13,234 5,332 1,489

findings.headline: Investment income forecast to fall 43% in 2025/26 to 2.88% of revenue, with no explanation provided
findings.detail: Net income from commercial and service investments is forecast to drop from 5.01% of revenue in 2024/25 to 2.88% in 2025/26 before recovering to 6.12% in 2026/27. The document presents this variance without explanation of the underlying cause.
findings.matters: Unexplained material volatility in investment returns affects net financial position; the magnitude of the dip and subsequent recovery suggests portfolio or market stress that warrants understanding.
findings.quote: Net income from commercial and service investments to net revenue stream as a % 5.01% 2.88% 6.12%

findings.headline: Capital expenditure budget more than doubles to £28.8m in 2026/27, with £17.6m slippage from prior year rolled forward
findings.detail: The 2026/27 capital budget of £28.8m compares to £13.4m forecast for 2025/26. Of this, £17.6m represents unspent allocation from 2025/26 being carried forward. This substantial capital program will require borrowing and generate financing costs across multiple years.
findings.matters: Large deferred capital spending creates multi-year debt obligations and limits forward financial flexibility; the scale of carry-forward suggests prior-year execution challenges.
findings.figures: £28.8m (2026/27 budget), £13.4m (2025/26 forecast), £17.6m slippage
findings.quote: Note 2: The figure includes £17.630m slippage form 2025/26 to be profiled to 2026-27

findings.headline: Financing costs rising to 8.35% of revenue stream by 2028/29, up from 5.93% in 2026/27
findings.detail: The proportion of financing costs to revenue stream is projected to grow from 5.93% in 2026/27 to 6.49% in 2027/28 and 8.35% in 2028/29. This reflects the council's capital program being financed through borrowing, showing an accelerating debt service burden on available revenue.
findings.matters: Escalating financing costs reduce the revenue available for service delivery and indicate rising debt service obligations; by 2028/29 financing costs will consume over 8% of net revenue.
findings.quote: Proportion of financing costs to revenue stream as a % 3.92% 4.88% 5.93% 6.49% 8.35%

findings.headline: Council has already taken out £8 million temporary borrowing for three-month cashflow management.
findings.detail: Beyond the existing £5m loan position, the council has secured additional temporary borrowing of £8m at 4.65% specifically to manage cashflow gaps. This is short-term bridge financing indicating near-term working capital constraints.
findings.matters: Active use of temporary borrowing for operational cashflow (not capital) is an indicator of liquidity pressure and inability to cover immediate obligations from operations or reserves.
findings.figures: £8.0 million temporary loan at 4.65% for 3 months (as of 31 December 2025)
findings.quote: The Council has since taken out an additional loan of £8.0 million for temporary cashflow purpose at a rate of 4.65% for 3 months.

findings.headline: Balance sheet resources declining from £78m to £72.8m over three years, with capital spending funded by borrowing rather than reserves.
findings.detail: The council's available resources (reserves and balances) are forecasted to decline steadily as capital expenditure is funded through external borrowing rather than drawdown of accumulated funds. This contrasts with strategies where capital is internally funded. The strategy explicitly states that borrowing will increase 'as reserve balances are reducing.'
findings.matters: Depleting reserves reduce the council's financial buffer and indicate increasing structural dependency on external financing, constraining future flexibility.
findings.figures: Balance sheet resources £78.0m (31 March 2025) declining to £72.8m forecast (31 March 2027) and £70.4m (31 March 2029)
findings.quote: Following on from the medium-term forecasts in table 2 above, the ten-year liability benchmark currently assumes capital expenditure will be funded by borrowing as reserve balances are reducing.

findings.headline: Council shifting from debt-free to active borrower, with £17.2m borrowing required by March 2027.
findings.detail: The council has been historically debt-free but now has a growing Capital Financing Requirement and plans to fund capital expenditure through borrowing. As of December 2025, it held £5m in loans and has already taken out an additional £8m temporary loan. The liability benchmark forecasts borrowing of £2.6m by March 2026, rising to £17.2m by March 2027.
findings.matters: This marks a structural shift in the council's financial position from a cash-generative position to external funding dependency, changing refinancing risk and creditworthiness profile.
findings.figures: £5.0 million in loans as of 31 December 2025; additional £8.0 million temporary loan at 4.65% for 3 months; borrowing requirement of £17.2 million expected by 31 March 2027
findings.quote: The Council has historically been largely debt free and has borrowed on a temporary basis to fund short term cash flow shortfalls.

findings.headline: Incomplete information provided to auditors — missing supporting documentation for opening balances and property floor plans
findings.detail: The auditor noted challenges obtaining complete listings for Collection Fund debtors and creditors, gaps in records supporting opening balances for debtors and creditors, and floor plans for several properties. This hampered the testing process.
findings.matters: Inability to obtain audit evidence suggests control weaknesses in record-keeping and financial management; contributed to auditor's inability to complete procedures.
findings.figures: Multiple areas affected: Collection Fund completeness, opening balances records, property documentation
findings.quote: There were, however, some challenges in obtaining certain information, in particular complete listings for Collection Fund debtors and creditors; gaps in the records supporting opening balances for debtors and creditors; and floor plans for several properties.

findings.headline: Revenue recognition classification errors — items misclassified between grant income and fees/charges
findings.detail: During testing of 46 items of Fees, Charges and Other Service Income, four items were incorrectly classified as Fees and Charges when they should have been recognised as grant income. Additional issues included income recognised in incorrect accounting periods and CIL income not captured in year-end accruals.
findings.matters: Misclassification of income between grant and fees affects reported revenue structure; completeness failures mean income may be omitted entirely.
findings.figures: 4 items misclassified in sample of 46; CIL completeness issues identified
findings.quote: 4 items were incorrectly classified within Fees and Charges and should have been recognised as grant income... A trivial amount of income had been recognised in the incorrect accounting period

findings.headline: £487k potential overstatement in debtors and creditors from CIL income recorded incorrectly
findings.detail: Two items were correctly treated as net nil within Fees and Charges as they relate to 2025/26 obligations, but were incorrectly recorded as both a debtor and a creditor in the accounts when the obligation does not exist until 2025/26. The council assessed the maximum potential impact as £487k.
findings.matters: Overstatement of both working capital balances affects reported cash position and debtor/creditor management.
findings.figures: £487k maximum potential impact
findings.quote: However, they had been incorrectly recorded as both a debtor and a creditor in the accounts, where the obligation does not exist until 25/26, resulting in an overstatement of both balances for the sample amount. The Council has assessed the maximum potential impact of this issue as £487k.

findings.headline: Segregation of duties control weakness in journals — users can self-authorise and hold both administrative and posting rights
findings.detail: Five individuals are authorised to approve journals; the auditor identified that three journals were posted by one approver. The system allows users to self-authorise journals, which is not good practice. This same issue was raised in the 2023/24 audit. Limited time between prior audit conclusion (February 2025) and 2024/25 year-end prevented remediation.
findings.matters: Weak journal controls create risk of undetected fraud or error in the accounting records, particularly given external scrutiny of council spending.
findings.figures: Five approved journal signatories; three journals posted by single approver
findings.quote: During our review of journal control design and implementation, we noted that some users have privileged access in the Business World finance system, allowing both administrative rights and journal-posting capabilities. This presents a segregation-of-duties risk... The system also allows users to self-authorise journals, which is not good practice and was previously raised in the 2023–24 audit.

findings.headline: £769.7k unadjusted pension asset error from Surrey Pension Fund valuation
findings.detail: The Surrey Pension Fund auditor identified a £26.542m understatement of Level 3 investments. Reigate and Banstead holds 2.9% of the fund, equating to £769.718k impact. Surrey Pension Fund confirmed no adjustment will be made. This error exceeds the trivial threshold and is below performance materiality.
findings.matters: Pension net asset/liability position is material to the accounts and affects reserves; this error affects reported financial position.
findings.figures: £769.718k (2.9% share of £26.542m fund error)
findings.quote: The Pension auditor for Surrey County Council Pension Fund identified an understatement of £26.542m for Level 3 investments held by Surrey Pension Fund as a whole. Reigate and Banstead Borough Council holds a 2.9% share of the Surrey Pension Fund's assets, which equates to an impact of approximately £769.718k. Surrey Pension Fund has confirmed that no adjustment will be made for this difference.

findings.headline: Cannot obtain assurance over £191m property valuations (Land and Buildings plus Investment Properties)
findings.detail: Of Land and Buildings (£157m at year-end), the auditor was unable to obtain assurance over site areas for 7 of 10 sampled assets. Errors were found in 3 of 10 samples where revaluation accounting did not comply with CIPFA guidance. For assets not revalued in current cycle (£14.051m), the auditor identified a potential £2.1m overstatement. For Investment Properties (£34m), the auditor could not obtain sufficient assurance over one of four material samples tested.
findings.matters: Property represents 60%+ of council balance sheet; lacking audit assurance over valuations means net asset position is unverified and potentially materially misstated.
findings.figures: £157m Land and Buildings, £34m Investment Properties, £2.1m potential overstatement identified, £14.051m unvalued since 2020-2024
findings.quote: As a result of the findings above, we have not been able to obtain sufficient assurance over the valuation of the full Land and Buildings population as at 31/03/2025. ... Consequently, we have not been able to obtain sufficient assurance over the valuation of the full Investment Property population as at 31/03/2025.

findings.headline: £0.8m unadjusted error in comprehensive income and expenditure statement
findings.detail: The auditor identified two adjustments totalling £0.8m to the financial statements that the council has chosen not to record. This amount impacts the reported outturn and reserves position.
findings.matters: Material unadjusted errors means reported financial position is materially misstated from what the auditor found.
findings.quote: We also identified two adjustments which officers have not adjusted the accounts; these have a £0.8m impact on the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement.

findings.headline: Council subsidiary Greensand Holdings Limited determined to be not a going concern
findings.detail: The subsidiary prepared year-end accounts in December 2024 on a going concern basis, but by November 2025 it was determined the subsidiary was no longer a going concern. The council updated its group accounts for 2024/25 in January 2026. The auditor has not undertaken planned audit procedures on group accounting due to time constraints.
findings.matters: A failing subsidiary represents a loss of council capital/investment and a potential financial liability that affects the group accounts and council reserves.
findings.figures: Subsidiary failure determined November 2025, accounts updated January 2026
findings.quote: The Council's subsidiary prepared year end accounts as at December 2024 for audit on a going concern basis. In November 2025, it was determined the subsidiary was not a going concern. The Council updated its group accounts for 2024/25 in January 2026 on the basis that the subsidiary is not a going concern.

findings.headline: Auditor will issue a disclaimer of opinion — cannot form an opinion on the financial statements
findings.detail: The auditor has been unable to undertake sufficient work to support an unmodified audit opinion due to inability to obtain assurance on opening balances from the prior year's disclaimed opinion. They intend to issue a disclaimer of opinion by the statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026. They have also been unable to conclude that the Annual Governance Statement is consistent with their knowledge.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion means the accounts cannot be relied upon by lenders or the council's finance leadership for decision-making.
findings.figures: Backstop date 27 February 2026
findings.quote: Owing to the challenges of undertaking an audit where the previous years' audits were subject to backstop-related disclaimed audit opinions, we have been unable to undertake sufficient work to support an unmodified audit opinion in advance of the backstop date of 27 February 2026. The limitations imposed by not having assurance on opening balances mean that we will be unable to form an opinion on the financial statements.

findings.headline: Council drawing £0.350m from General Fund Reserves to balance 2026/27 budget.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget requires a £0.350m contribution from General Fund Reserves to achieve balance. General Fund reserves are forecast at £2.427m on 1st April 2026, which is above the 10% policy minimum (£2.361m), but the need to use reserves to balance the current budget indicates structural deficit.
findings.matters: Using reserves to balance the budget is unsustainable beyond one or two years; indicates the underlying budget position does not cover costs from recurring income.
findings.figures: £0.350m reserve contribution; General Fund Reserve forecast £2.427m (10% threshold = £2.361m)
findings.quote: Therefore, a general transfer from reserves is required to fulfil the legal requirement of the Council to agree a balanced budget.

findings.headline: Council merges into unitary authority 1st April 2027 with reorganisation costs "not directly quantifiable at this stage".
findings.detail: This is the final budget before Reigate and Banstead ceases to exist and merges with Tandridge, Mole Valley, Epsom and Ewell, Elmbridge and parts of Surrey County Council. The council identifies "initial cost implications" for the merger including "information gathering, cohesion of IT systems, branding and restructuring" but states these costs are "not directly quantifiable at this stage".
findings.matters: Unquantified one-off costs in the final year before major structural change; difficult to assess true budget position.
findings.figures: Costs not quantified
findings.quote: As part of integration and implementation process, there will be various costs involved e.g. information gathering, cohesion of IT systems, branding and restructuring.

findings.headline: Full Business Rates Reset from April 2026 with unquantified impact: "At this moment we do not know the full effect of this on the Council's budget, and this remains a risk."
findings.detail: The Government announced a full reset of the Business Rates retention system (first time in over a decade) with new multi-tiered multipliers. The council explicitly states the impact is unknown. The NNDR1 form has not been finalised (due 31 January 2026); the budget uses published baseline funding levels. Forecast Business Rates decline £0.314m in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Major system change creates income budget uncertainty in the council's final year before merger, difficult to model.
findings.figures: 2025/26 Business Rates £3.229m; 2026/27 forecast £2.915m (£0.314m reduction)
findings.quote: At this moment we do not know the full effect of this on the Council's budget, and this remains a risk.

findings.headline: £4.5m Harlequin Theatre RAAC remediation approved, but longer-term revenue impact is explicitly unquantified.
findings.detail: The council approved £4.5m capital for removal of Reinforced Autoclaved Aerated Concrete at the Harlequin Theatre. A procurement process is underway for a third-party operator. The 2026/27 budget reflects reduced premises costs while building works are underway, but the paper states: "the longer-term impact on the revenue budget for the running of both venues is unknown at this stage".
findings.matters: Large capital commitment with unquantified future revenue implications creates budget risk, particularly given the council merges in April 2027.
findings.figures: £4.5m capital budget approved; capital programme includes £3m of annual maintenance works profiled 2027/28 to 2030/31
findings.quote: However, the longer-term impact on the revenue budget for the running of both venues is unknown at this stage.

findings.headline: £0.509m of homelessness funding removed from ring-fenced grant and merged into un-ringfenced Revenue Support Grant.
findings.detail: The Provisional Local Government Finance Settlement changed how homelessness services are funded. £0.509m that was previously a dedicated ring-fenced grant is now part of the un-ringfenced Revenue Support Grant. The council is maintaining equivalent funding for 2026/27 but explicitly flags that it will "monitor changing service demands and future funding announcements closely".
findings.matters: Loss of ring-fenced status removes funding certainty and creates discretion over allocation; signals vulnerability if overall RSG is constrained.
findings.figures: £0.509m funding change
findings.quote: Due to the overall relative financial health of this Council, for 2026/27 there will be an equivalent level of funding for Homelessness services as in 2025/26, however changing service demands and future funding announcements will continue to be monitored closely.

findings.headline: Q2 monitoring shows £1.073m revenue overspend for 2025/26, with Redhill Distribution Centre showing £0.932m deficit.
findings.detail: At Q2 (30 September 2025), the council is forecasting a revenue overspend of £1.073m against the original £23.167m budget. Property Services has a £0.932m deficit at Redhill Distribution Centre; Housing Benefits shows £0.307m overspend due to payments not being fully funded by central government subsidy.
findings.matters: Active in-year budget overruns indicate management challenges; the Redhill Distribution Centre deficit is an ongoing commercial property loss.
findings.figures: £1.073m total projected overspend; £0.932m Redhill Distribution Centre deficit; £0.307m Housing Benefits overspend
findings.quote: As at the end of Quarter 2 (30 September), there was a projected overspend against the Original Budget for the year of £1.073 million. This comprised a £0.766m forecast overspend within Service budgets, and a £0.307 million overspend within Central budgets.

findings.headline: Council now borrowing externally instead of using internal cash balances to fund capital.
findings.detail: The council has shifted from self-financing capital expenditure through internal cash balances to external borrowing. Treasury management budget increases £1.041m, with £0.370m allocated for interest payable on new borrowing and £0.500m budget pressure from reduced investment income due to lower cash balances and lower forecast interest rates.
findings.matters: External borrowing increases exposure to interest rate risk and commits future revenues to debt service, signalling deterioration in the council's liquidity position.
findings.figures: £0.370m for interest payable on borrowing; £0.500m reduction in interest receivable; Treasury Management budget increase of £1.041m
findings.quote: Whereas previously the Council has benefitted from using its internal cash balances to finance Capital Expenditure, it is now in a position where it will need to borrow, with £0.370 million now set aside to finance interest payments.

findings.headline: One-off £1.890m pension actuarial gain in 2026/27 masks underlying cost pressures
findings.detail: A secondary pension contribution benefit of £1.890m appears only in 2026/27 and does not recur in any subsequent year (shown as 0.000 thereafter). This one-off actuarial valuation gain helps balance the current year but will not be available to offset costs in future years.
findings.matters: The one-off nature of this pension benefit means it temporarily improves 2026/27 position but creates a cliff-edge when it expires, making underlying structural pressures larger than currently visible.
findings.quote: Actuarial valuation - Secondary Pension contributions 0.000 (1.890) 0.000 0.000 0.000

findings.headline: MTFP acknowledged as incomplete; updated version due summer 2026
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that the MTFP presented has not been fully reworked "due to time constraints" and an updated version is hoped to be presented in summer 2026. It notes the current presentation does not yet show all key budget lines as totals year-on-year.
findings.matters: Current projections are incomplete and subject to material change; 2027/28 deficit and onwards may shift when figures are updated.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: Due to time constraints, it has not been possible to re-work the MTFP any further at this stage – it is hoped an updated version will be presented in the Summer of 2026

findings.headline: Base salary costs rising 25.6% over the MTFP period (£6.833m increase)
findings.detail: The document notes that salary costs are "proportionately the largest single item of Council expenditure" and projects them rising from £26.674m in 2025/26 to £33.507m by 2029/30. The 2026/27 year alone sees an 8.6% jump to £28.988m, reflecting accumulated pay inflation assumptions.
findings.matters: Salary is the council's largest cost item and is growing faster than apparent funding increases; pay inflation assumptions are a material driver of the emerging deficit.
findings.quote: Base Council salary costs - year-on-year totals 26.674 28.988 30.436 31.943 33.507

findings.headline: £0.350m transfer from reserves needed to fund 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: The council is explicitly drawing £0.350m from reserves in 2026/27 to achieve a balanced budget, and explicitly states there are no planned reserve draws for subsequent years. This reveals an underlying structural pressure in the current-year budget.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund current expenditure reduces financial flexibility and suggests underlying cost-to-funding mismatch before the formal gap appears.
findings.figures: £0.350 million
findings.quote: There is a planned transfer from reserves of £0.350 million to fund the 2026/27 budget.

findings.headline: Forecast funding gap grows from £0.753m in 2027/28 to £2.195m by 2029/30
findings.detail: The MTFP balances 2026/27 but reveals a materializing structural deficit from 2027/28 onwards. The gap nearly triples over the forecast period, indicating growing cost-to-funding mismatch. The council has not yet stated how this gap will be closed (savings, borrowing, or reserve depletion).
findings.matters: A growing unfunded deficit is a credit risk signal for lenders and signals future budget pressure requiring significant intervention by the finance director.
findings.figures: FORECAST FUNDING GAP 0.000 0.000 0.753 1.497 2.195
findings.quote: FORECAST FUNDING GAP 0.000 0.000 0.753 1.497 2.195

findings.paper_title: Observations on Budget Proposals 2026/27 - Budget Scrutiny Panel Report
findings.headline: Staff pay negotiations unresolved; budget assumes 2.5% but unions seeking more
findings.detail: A 2.5% pay increase had been previously agreed for 2025/26 and the same was offered for 2026/27. Unions had requested higher increases and negotiations were ongoing at the time of the Panel meeting on 26 November 2025. The Chief Executive was unsure whether agreement would be reached before Christmas. The Panel noted this as a risk.
findings.matters: Unresolved pay negotiations create risk of budget overrun if unions secure higher settlements than the assumed 2.5%
findings.figures: 2.5% pay increase assumed; unions requesting higher increases; negotiations ongoing
findings.quote: the Chief Executive reported that a staff pay increase of 2.5% had previously been agreed for the current year and that the same had been offered for 2026/27. Unions had requested higher increases and negotiations were ongoing. The Chief Executive was unsure whether the pay increase would be agreed before Christmas. The Panel noted this as a risk.

findings.paper_title: Observations on Budget Proposals 2026/27 - Budget Scrutiny Panel Report
findings.headline: Property and rental income assumptions not yet confirmed; panel flagged as material risk
findings.detail: The budget assumes that loss of income from properties and facilities will be minimised through re-letting. However, the Council has not yet confirmed these properties will be re-let. The Panel Chair noted this should be treated as a risk. Additionally, planning income remains below budget despite improvement in the current year.
findings.matters: Unconfirmed income assumptions create risk of further budget shortfalls if properties remain vacant or income targets not met
findings.figures: property/facilities income at risk; planning income still below budget
findings.quote: It was confirmed that the loss of income for properties and facilities had not been included in the budget for 2026/27 as officers had plans in train to minimise the loss of income and were confident of re-letting the properties. The Chair noted that this should be treated as a risk.

findings.paper_title: Observations on Budget Proposals 2026/27 - Budget Scrutiny Panel Report
findings.headline: Council Tax freeze decision will cost new unitary council £2.2m in cumulative lost income by 2029/30
findings.detail: The Executive is not increasing Council Tax for 2026/27. A 2.99% increase would generate approximately £516k (75% of the current budget gap). The Panel noted that forgoing the increase will put the new unitary council at a permanent funding disadvantage reaching £2.2m by 2029/30. The Panel recommended the Executive carefully justify this decision and requested it be set out clearly.
findings.matters: A decision to freeze council tax will create a structural income problem for the successor unitary council, materially worsening its financial position within four years
findings.figures: 2.99% increase would yield £516k (75% of budget gap); permanent disadvantage to unitary of £2.2m by 2029/30
findings.quote: An increase of 2.99% would bring approximately £516k into the revenue budget, equating to around 75% of the current budget gap... Applying no increase will put the new unitary council at a permanent funding disadvantage which would reach £2.2million by 2029/30 in lost income.

findings.paper_title: Observations on Budget Proposals 2026/27 - Budget Scrutiny Panel Report
findings.headline: Council likely to move into external borrowing for first time, ending historic debt-free position
findings.detail: The Panel noted that the Council had historically been debt-free and funded assets through internal borrowing. The Panel noted this 'was likely to change later in this financial year as cash reserves are depleted with the continuing capital programme' and that 'the Council may move into an external borrowing position.' This represents a fundamental shift in the council's financial structure and risk profile.
findings.matters: Transition from internal to external borrowing signals reserve exhaustion and is a material change in financial risk profile and cost of capital for future funding
findings.figures: historic debt-free status; shift to external borrowing forecast in current/next financial year
findings.quote: The Panel noted that the Council had previously been able to fund its assets by internal borrowing and has historically been the only debt-free authority in Surrey. The Panel noted that this was likely to change later in this financial year as cash reserves are depleted with the continuing capital programme, and in particular items such as the Housing Delivery & Community Assets Reserve is applied to specific projects.

findings.paper_title: Observations on Budget Proposals 2026/27 - Budget Scrutiny Panel Report
findings.headline: Housing Benefit Subsidy creates £1m annual funding gap on £22m total commitment
findings.detail: The Council receives £1m less in government funding than it actually pays out on housing benefit, and the subsidy totals £22m. This structural mismatch is flagged as a significant risk and is being addressed partially through a £0.671m reserve drawdown rather than base budget solution, deferring the problem.
findings.matters: A recurring structural funding gap of this scale (5% of a £22m programme) is a material financial risk that cannot be sustained through reserve drawdowns alone
findings.figures: £1m annual government funding shortfall; £22m total Housing Benefit Subsidy; £0.671m drawn from reserves to manage in 2026/27
findings.quote: the Council receives £1million less in government funding than it pays out and as it totals £22million this presents a significant risk

findings.paper_title: Observations on Budget Proposals 2026/27 - Budget Scrutiny Panel Report
findings.headline: Council to draw £0.683m from reserves to balance 2026/27 budget, with General Fund Reserve falling to minimum policy level
findings.detail: The General Fund Reserve is projected to fall from £3.5m on 1 April 2025 to £2.3m at 31 March 2026, reaching the minimum 10% level required under the Council's policy. An additional £0.671m is being drawn specifically to fund Housing Benefit Subsidy pressures. Overall reserves are forecast to drop £4m in the current year. The Panel recommended further analysis of reserve balances and their forecast usage.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion to minimum levels indicates the budget is not sustainable without drawing down reserves, leaving the council with no financial buffer for unexpected costs or income shortfalls
findings.figures: General Fund Reserve falling from £3.5m to £2.3m; £0.683m drawdown; £0.671m Housing Benefit drawdown; overall £4m reserve reduction forecast
findings.quote: The General Fund Reserve is projected to fall from £3.5million on 1 April 2025 to a forecast of £2.3million at 31 March 2026, as the result of a projected budget deficit in the current year. This puts the General Fund Reserve at the minimum 10% level required under the Council's policy.

news_drafts.lead: Non-execution of a board resolution to sell assets suggests valuation or market difficulties and raises questions about capital asset management and effectiveness of governance oversight.
